fix(resolve): "did you mean" must not offer the shortest fragment first (S22)

`nearMatches` had no test. Every one of its callers prints the whole list verbatim as
`did you mean a, b, c?`, so its ordering is the advice an agent acts on.

Three defects, each confirmed by probe before the edit:

**A substring scored 0 — the same score as an exact match.** The tiebreak is
alphabetical, so `nearMatches('graphs', ['graph','graphs'])` returned
`['graph','graphs']`: the exact match second, behind the prefix of itself.

**Containment had no length floor.** `cl.includes(lower) || lower.includes(cl)` means
any fragment of the query is a perfect match. `nearMatches('test', ['e','test-writer'])`
returned `e` first, and the printed message was `did you mean e, test-writer?` — a
name an agent can install. There was nothing between the two candidates to choose
from except the length of what was typed.

**The bound did not shrink with the query.** Three edits is a typo in `slice-commmit`.
Three edits to a four-character query is a different string, and offering it breaks the
rule in this file's own header: a suggestion that far away is noise. `cov` was offered
for `coverage-hunt`.

The fix: exact is 0, a candidate containing the query is 1 (a prefix is not zero edits,
which is the whole of the first defect), a candidate inside the query is 1 only when it
is at least half as long, and the bound is
`max(1, min(max, floor(len / 3)))` — which also means `max` is a ceiling rather than a
dial, and can only tighten. A test that asserted otherwise would have been asserting a
behaviour that does not exist.

Five tests, three mutations, each caught by the assertion written for it: restoring the
0, dropping the half-length floor, and flattening the bound. Two of the five fixtures
were wrong before they were right — transpositions are two edits, not one, so a cap
test built on them was asserting an exclusion — and the comments now say so. 796/796.
